title: Field in the frame: agricultural fires from above
summary:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 16 April 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-03496-x

War can have wide-ranging environmental impacts, including on agricultural production. Professors Gong and Lin and colleagues analysed satellite imagery over agricultural areas in five provinces of eastern Ukraine from 2019-2022. They found that production of wheat, sunflower, and rapeseed in these regions has declined by more than thirty percent in the subsequent growing season since the beginning of the Russia-Ukraine war. This work demonstrates the devastating impact that war can have upon agriculture and therefore food security worldwide.

summary:
Nature Sustainability, Published online: 27 March 2026; doi:10.1038/s41893-026-01793-z

Climate change, particularly intensifying droughts, is often blamed for wildfires across the Gran Chaco, a vast South American dry woodland. An analysis of over 30 years of fire patterns, however, reveals that the majority of fires are driven by agricultural expansion and deforestation.

summary:

summary:

title: Rapid subsurface warming in the subpolar North Atlantic from freshening
summary:
Nature Communications, Published online: 27 March 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-70635-5

The North Atlantic subpolar gyre has freshened over recent decades, a trend projected to intensify under continued global warming. This study shows that the resulting increase in stratification drives ~ 1°C subsurface warming within a decade and a reorganisation of oceanic circulation that can enhance surface warming in the Nordic Seas.

summary:

title: Datacenters as core infrastructure of urban AI
summary:

title: Understanding kampungs as critical urban infrastructures
summary:
Nature Cities, Published online: 27 March 2026; doi:10.1038/s44284-026-00428-w

Urban kampungs in Indonesia are more than ‘informal settlements’. This framing broadens the understanding of urban infrastructure beyond technical systems.

title: Urban nature equity must consider cultural nuances
summary:
npj Urban Sustainability, Published online: 12 March 2026; doi:10.1038/s42949-026-00352-x

Culture profoundly influences the way a person engages with nature. As cities rapidly increase in cultural diversity, achieving universal equity in access to nature and the benefits that flow from it will depend on meaningful consideration of this diversity in urban design. Current approaches to urban planning and design tend to be implicitly monocultural, which may diminish equity of access and reproduce entrenched epistemological and material conditions that contribute to power imbalances and dictate whose preferences are reflected in urban nature spaces. To move toward culturally inclusive urban nature design demands explicit efforts be made in policy and practice to embrace the contextual, dynamic and multifaceted nature of culture and resist the implicit adoption of monocultural urban nature designs. We discuss the consequences of superficial cultural inclusion attempts and propose three key recommendations for taking a culturally-conscious approach towards urban nature equity.

title: Strong earthquakes on the French-Italian Mediterranean Riviera
summary:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 20 March 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-03407-0

A joint analysis of seismological, geodetic and geological data constrains the recurrence time of large, potentially tsunamigenic and destructive earthquakes on the Ligurian Fault on the Mediterranean French-Italian border to between 2,353 and 9,484 years

title: The Martian mid-latitude subsurface ice is the remnant of a past ice sheet
summary:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 21 March 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-03418-x

Mars planetary climate model simulations show that mid-latitude ice accumulated around 630,000 years ago, at 35° obliquity, matching the depth and spatial variation of today’s buried ice and suggesting this ice layer contains a record of the retreating past surface ice sheet

title: A combination of social media and satellite data improves flood monitoring in China
summary:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 21 March 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-03403-4

In China, about half of the flood events were unobservable by remote sensing, capturing mostly riverine flooding in open areas, while social media fills gaps in densely populated urban settings, according to a social sensing framework that combines satellite precipitation mapping and Sina Weibo posts

title: Land-atmosphere feedbacks and anthropogenic greenhouse gas forcing intensify subseasonal drought-to-pluvial abrupt transitions
summary:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 23 March 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-03371-9

Abrupt transitions from drought to extreme precipitation occur more often under higher atmospheric greenhouse gas levels, and are favored through the influence of soil moisture deficits on convective precipitation, revealed by a global assessment based on reanalysis data and climate model projections.

title: Lake expansion underpinned the Silk Road prosperity during a drought period
summary:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 24 March 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-03415-0

Enhanced meltwater in arid Central Asia during a warm and dry period in the Tang dynasty between CE 600 and 900 created well-watered corridors and supported Silk Road prosperity, according to a high-resolution lake-level record from Jili Lake, China
